endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: For devices built on third-party foundation models, changes to the underlying model may be initiated by the third-party model developer rather than the device manufacturer. How can a manufacturer detect, evaluate, and respond to such changes in a timely manner?

endorsements.title: Governing medical AI under the EU AI Act: an integrated compliance-by-design framework
endorsements.quote: The allocation of monitoring and change-control responsibility between the GPAI provider, the downstream high-risk provider, and the deployer therefore becomes a substantive governance question taken up at Stages 7 and 8 (Sections 8.7 – 8.8 ).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in reproductive endocrinology: an in-depth longitudinal analysis of ChatGPTv4's month-by-month interpretation and adherence to clinical guidelines for diminished ovarian reserve
evidence.outcome: Change in ChatGPT-4 guideline-question accuracy and completeness between baseline and two-month follow-up
evidence.effect: Open-ended accuracy rose from 5.38±0.71 to 5.74±0.51 (max 6) and completeness from 2.57±0.52 to 2.85±0.36 (max 3), p<0.001. Multiple-choice accuracy rose from 98.2% to 100%. True/false stayed at 100%.
evidence.quote: Open-ended question responses exhibited significant positive enhancements, with accuracy scores increasing from an average of 5.38 ± 0.71 to 5.74 ± 0.51 (max: 6.0) and completeness scores from 2.57 ± 0.52 to 2.85 ± 0.36 (max: 3.0).

evidence.title: Feasibility of AI-powered assessment scoring: Can large language models replace human raters?
evidence.outcome: LLM scoring reliability and discrepancies before versus after public release of the model
evidence.effect: After public release, reliability decreased notably (ICC = -0.046 for BVMT-R Trial 3) and average scoring discrepancies rose (SDMT from 0.05 to 6.79).
evidence.quote: After ChatGPT-4.5 was publicly released, reliability decreased notably (e.g. ICC = -0.046 for BVMT-R Trial 3), and average scoring discrepancies per test increased (e.g. SDMT = 6.79).

evidence.title: The temporal changes in GPT-4 performance on UKMLA practice questions: educational and clinical implications
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 accuracy on UKMLA questions across two time points after vendor-side updates
evidence.effect: Accuracy changed after vendor updates, improving from 88.0 to 93.7% with MCQ and 68.1 to 81.7% without MCQ; the changes were not all statistically significant, and drivers are opaque.
evidence.quote: GPT-4's performance improved across all question categories from round one to round two, most notably in management questions without MCQ options (+23.30%), though these differences were not statistically significant.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested a process for detecting, evaluating, or responding to developer-initiated changes in third-party foundation models, and three offline studies show that model outputs shift between versions, in one case toward much lower reliability. The recommendation rests on regulatory reasoning and documented hazard rather than evidence that the safeguard works.

perspectives.view: No study tests a monitoring or change-response process. Three hazard studies, all offline or benchmark designs at evidence levels 4 and 5, report that model outputs changed between time points. These studies show that the problem exists. They do not show that any detection process catches it, so certainty about the practice cannot be rated.

After a model's public release, one study found scoring reliability fell to ICC = -0.046 for BVMT-R Trial 3, and average SDMT scoring discrepancies rose from 0.05 to 6.79. Two other studies found accuracy rose after updates. Because the direction of change varied, validation done once at deployment may not predict later behavior.

The UK benchmark study reported that the drivers of accuracy changes after vendor updates were opaque, and not all changes reached statistical significance. If developers do not disclose what changed, deploying organizations may detect shifts only by rerunning their own test sets. No study has measured the workload or the detection rate of such retesting.

Both endorsing sources treat responsibility for upstream changes as unsettled. The regulatory discussion paper poses detection and response as an open question. The EU AI Act commentary describes the division of monitoring and change control among the model provider, the downstream device maker, and the deployer as a governance question. Neither source cites evidence that a specific process works.

commentary.research_gap: Prospective studies are needed that deploy specific monitoring methods, such as fixed sentinel test sets, version pinning, or contractual change notifications, in live clinical tools built on third-party models. These studies should measure time to detect a change, the share of meaningful changes missed, staff effort, and whether detection prevents errors that reach patients.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the three hazard studies reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations; two did not report a setting and one used a UK exam benchmark. All relied on guideline questions, exam items, or test protocols, so it is unknown whether upstream model changes affect outputs differently for non-English or plain-language inputs, and monitoring test sets built from standard English content may miss such shifts.
